text: This past August, I did something I had never done before: released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories about settings mysteriously changing during operating system updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change during macOS updates (see “ SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes ,” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration changes after users install updates. Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is tell you something you didn’t want to know. I wasn’t confident enough to call that first version 1.0, so, like countless developers before me, I hedged by releasing 1.0b26 alongside that article. Since then, I have been adding to and refining SetShot, and although there is plenty more that could be done, I encourage you to download and try the official SetShot 1.0 , which is free and open source . Cue the confetti and balloons! When you take a snapshot, SetShot scans 20 sources of macOS system data, including over 500 preference files. It currently recognizes over 830 settings and knows to ignore as background noise over 1750 other items that macOS changes on its own. You can compare any two snapshots—usually the most recent two—to see what changed between them, or compare a snapshot against a built-in baseline captured from a clean install of macOS 15 Sequoia, macOS 26 Tahoe, or macOS 27 Golden Gate. Each comparison lists every recognized change with its title, its location in System Settings, and its before-and-after values. Where possible, an Open in Settings button takes you directly to the appropriate pane in System Settings. If something seems off about the setting’s title, path, or values, you can click Submit Feedback to help me improve the SetShot knowledge base. Changes that SetShot doesn’t yet recognize appear in a separate section with their raw technical names and values. If you think one is a real setting, click Submit to send it to me for addition to the knowledge base. Along the way, SetShot maintains the Journal, which is a chronological log of all recognized changes across your comparisons. Because your first snapshot is compared against the baseline, the Journal starts out with all your existing customizations. You can even export the Journal to HTML or Markdown to use as a checklist when setting up a new Mac to match your current one. (SetShot doesn’t write settings, so you’ll still be flipping switches by hand.) You can take snapshots manually whenever you like, but SetShot can also take them automatically on a schedule you set in its Settings view. By default, SetShot deletes scheduled snapshots that contain no changes. When a scheduled snapshot finds a recognized change, SetShot displays a notification that you can click to run the comparison. I run snapshots frequently throughout the day for testing, but for most people, a daily check is sufficient. If you’re running one of the betas, choose SetShot > Check for Updates to get 1.0. Versions before 1.0b32 biffed their automatic update checks, so they won’t find it on their own. I have released eight beta updates since 1.0b26 with a slew of new features, interface tweaks, and bug fixes. You can read the gory details in the release notes , but the highlights include: Although I haven’t caught Apple changing a setting behind my back during an update, the betas have produced a few stories that show how macOS stores settings and just how much is going on in the background on our Macs. When Mark Nagata, the coordinator of our Japanese translation team, first ran SetShot, his initial comparison reported 33,000 changes. Nearly all of them came from one file, com.apple.audio.InfoHelper.plist , which caches what each installed Audio Unit plug-in can do. Macs without audio plug-ins, like all of mine, lack that file, so SetShot didn’t know about it beforehand. Once I trained SetShot to ignore that file as noise, those changes disappeared from the comparison. macOS did silently change one setting, although it wasn’t during an update. One day back in September, SetShot’s scheduled comparison reported that my default Web browser had changed from Arc to Safari. I had not made that change, but clicking links in other apps did in fact open them in Safari, even though System Settings > Desktop & Dock still reported Arc as the default Web browser. I don’t understand what happened here, but changing the default in System Settings to Brave and back to Arc fixed it. When I upgraded to the beta of macOS 27.3, my first comparison in SetShot revealed hundreds of changes relating to Siri as Apple moved settings between preference files. I have marked them all as noise now, so you won’t see them, but it was interesting to get a glimpse of Apple moving things around in preparation for new features. SetShot also featured in an amusing archaeological settings dig. While doing some testing, John Gruber of Daring Fireball changed his highlight color from the very specific blue he chose decades ago, but he was dismayed to discover he couldn’t restore his custom color because Apple had changed how the color picker works. SetShot showed his old RGB string changing to the word “Other,” which confirmed the change but didn’t help him undo it. He suggested that SetShot should report the defaults key so he didn’t have to figure out the appropriate defaults write command. It’s now on the list to look into. I have various ideas for features to add, and several more have come from early users. In no particular order, they include: My enthusiasm for adding new features will be proportional to how much input and support I get from users. SetShot is free and open source because I harbor no illusions about its commercial potential, but I’m more likely to keep working on it if people who find it useful become TidBITS members and share their thoughts with me. Give it a try !
